readyRule: An objective is Ready when its question is answered correctly, either the first time or in its return form. questions.stem: Keys arrive in sorted order. How do a plain BST and an AVL tree compare for search?
questions.hint: This question checks whether you can link the insertion order to the height of the tree and the cost of a search. A search needs at most one comparison for each level.

options.text: The plain BST becomes a chain with O(n) search. The AVL tree is rebalanced after each insertion, so its height and its search cost stay O(log n).
options.explanation: Sorted input is the worst case for a plain BST, and the AVL rule is designed to prevent it.

options.text: Both give O(log n) search, because both are binary search trees.
options.explanation: A plain BST has no balance guarantee, and sorted input makes it a chain.

options.text: Both become chains, because sorted input always produces a chain.
options.explanation: The AVL tree rotates as keys arrive, so it never becomes a chain.

questions.stem: A plain BST with 1,000 keys may need 1,000 comparisons for one search. An AVL tree with the same keys needs at most 14. Why?
questions.hint: This question checks whether you can explain what an AVL tree guarantees. Rebalancing keeps the height short, so the search path stays short too.

options.text: The insertion order can make a plain BST a chain of 1,000 levels. The AVL rule keeps the height at most 13, so a search needs at most 14 comparisons.
options.explanation: The AVL rule limits the height, and the height limits the number of comparisons.

options.text: The AVL tree uses balance factors during the search to skip levels.
The plain BST visits every node during a search.
options.explanation: A search follows one path in both trees. The path in the plain BST can just be much longer.

questions.stem: Enter the balance factors of 20 and 30, and then decide whether this is an AVL tree.
questions.hint: This question checks heights and balance factors. Height counts the edges down to a leaf, and the balance factor is h(right) − h(left), where an empty branch counts as −1.

wrongAnswers.feedback: The sign is reversed. The balance factor is the height of the right branch minus the height of the left branch. Node 20 has an empty right branch (height −1) and a left branch of height 1, so its balance factor is −1 − 1 = −2. A taller left branch gives a negative number.
An empty branch has height −1, not 0. Node 20 has an empty right branch (height −1) and a left branch of height 1, so its balance factor is −1 − 1 = −2.

The sign is reversed. The balance factor is the height of the right branch minus the height of the left branch. Node 30 has a right branch of height 0 and a left branch of height 2, so its balance factor is 0 − 2 = −2. A taller left branch gives a negative number.

feedback.correct: Node 20 has an empty right branch (height −1) and a left branch of height 1, so its balance factor is −1 − 1 = −2. Node 30 has a right branch of height 0 and a left branch of height 2, so its balance factor is 0 − 2 = −2. This is not an AVL tree, because nodes 20, 30 and 60 break the AVL rule.
feedback.incorrect: Node 20 has an empty right branch (height −1) and a left branch of height 1, so its balance factor is −1 − 1 = −2. Node 30 has a right branch of height 0 and a left branch of height 2, so its balance factor is 0 − 2 = −2. This is not an AVL tree, because nodes 20, 30 and 60 break the AVL rule.

questions.stem: 25 has just been inserted. Find n, name the case and perform the rotation or rotations.
questions.hint: This question checks whether you can carry out the rotation or rotations. The child moves up around its parent, and the child's inner subtree changes sides.

wrongAnswers.feedback: One rotation about 50 does not fix an inside case, so the tree is still unbalanced. First do a left rotation about the child, 20, and then rotate about 50.
For an inside case, rotate about n's child first, which turns it into an outside case. Then rotate about n.
Rotate towards the shorter branch. If n's left branch is too tall, the final rotation about n is a right rotation. If n's right branch is too tall, it is a left rotation.

feedback.correct: Node 50 is n, with a balance factor of −2. This is Case 2 (LR). The fix is a left rotation about 20, followed by a right rotation about 50. The result is 30(20(10, 25), 50(·, 60)).
feedback.incorrect: Node 50 is n, with a balance factor of −2. This is Case 2 (LR). The fix is a left rotation about 20, followed by a right rotation about 50. The result is 30(20(10, 25), 50(·, 60)).

questions.stem: An online exam system stores 30,000 student numbers. Numbers are added at registration in increasing order and looked up thousands of times during an exam. Which structure should the system use, and why?
questions.hint: This question checks whether you can recognise a good fit for an AVL tree. An AVL tree suits data that is searched often and must stay in sorted order.

options.text: A plain BST. It is simpler, and BST search is always O(log n).
options.explanation: Increasing numbers make a plain BST a chain, with O(n) search.

options.text: An unsorted list. Adding a number is O(1), which matters most here.
options.explanation: Lookups happen thousands of times, and each one would be O(n) in an unsorted list.

options.text: An AVL tree. Frequent lookups need guaranteed O(log n) search, and increasing numbers would make a plain BST a chain.
options.explanation: Lookups dominate, and the order of arrival is the worst case for a plain BST.

questions.stem: What is the strongest reason to use an AVL tree for a spell checker's word list?
questions.hint: This question checks whether you can justify the choice from the properties of an AVL tree. It guarantees O(log n) search, at the cost of extra work on updates.

options.text: AVL trees use less memory than other trees.
options.explanation: They store a height in every node, so they use slightly more memory.

options.text: AVL search uses balance factors to find words faster.
Words are looked up constantly and may be loaded in alphabetical order, and the AVL tree keeps every lookup O(log n).
options.explanation: Frequent lookups and possibly sorted input are the two reasons that matter here.
